Because these Lighthouse trade-offs are hypotheses rather than measured results, the telemetry also needs checks for simulator artifacts. A fixed-latency queuing model, omitted DRAM refresh cycles, or an unconstrained register-file assumption in the compiler backend can each manufacture an apparent mechanism that exists only inside the model. Even on real hardware, paired profiler counters show why a single intermediate metric such as warp occupancy cannot serve as a universal causal story for kernel speedups (@fig-ch07-kernelagent-ncu-counterfactual).

![**Faster retained GPU kernels do not move intermediate profiler counters in one uniform direction.** Paired Round 1 (open circles) and fastest retained round (filled squares) across `{python} ka11_n` KernelBench tasks profiled with NVIDIA Nsight Compute in the KernelAgent artifacts [@Cheng2025KernelAgentArtifacts]: (a) kernel execution time relative to Round 1, (b) achieved warp occupancy, and (c) sustained DRAM throughput. In MaxPool 3D and 3D transposed convolution, the fastest retained kernel achieves lower execution time alongside lower achieved occupancy, whereas in matrix–vector multiplication both occupancy and DRAM throughput rise steeply.](images/fig-ch07-kernelagent-ncu-counterfactual){#fig-ch07-kernelagent-ncu-counterfactual width="100%" fig-alt="Three-panel dumbbell chart comparing Round 1 and the fastest retained optimization round across five KernelBench tasks on relative kernel time, achieved occupancy, and DRAM throughput. Latency drops or holds nearly steady across all five tasks, while occupancy rises sharply for matrix-vector multiplication but falls for MaxPool 3D and transposed 3D convolution."}

Across those `{python} ka11_n` paired Nsight Compute profiles [@Cheng2025KernelAgentArtifacts], matrix–vector multiplication lowers execution time from `{python} ka11_mv_t1`\ ms to `{python} ka11_mv_tb`\ ms while raising achieved warp occupancy from `{python} ka11_mv_occ1`% to `{python} ka11_mv_occb`% and DRAM throughput from `{python} ka11_mv_dram1`% to `{python} ka11_mv_dramb`%. In MaxPool 3D, by contrast, the fastest retained round cuts execution time from `{python} ka11_mp_t1`\ ms to `{python} ka11_mp_tb`\ ms (`{python} ka11_mp_rel` of Round 1 time) while achieved occupancy falls from `{python} ka11_mp_occ1`% to `{python} ka11_mp_occb`% and DRAM throughput rises from `{python} ka11_mp_dram1`% to `{python} ka11_mp_dramb`%; in 3D transposed convolution, occupancy similarly drops from `{python} ka11_tc_occ1`% to `{python} ka11_tc_occb`% as latency nearly halves. Because occupancy falls in MaxPool 3D and 3D transposed convolution, higher occupancy cannot explain every speedup. These paired endpoint profiles show only co-movement across distinct kernel implementations; they do not isolate a mechanism.

A mechanism counts as supported only when controlled contrasts and model checks support it, and even then the conclusion remains scoped to the model and its identification assumptions. Without such contrasts, the mechanism stays contradicted, unresolved, or untested according to @tbl-outcome-mechanism, while a supported top-line outcome can still be retained separately.

## Combining Independent Checks to Catch Blind Spots {#sec-independent-checks-and-correlated-errors}

A complete requirement map identifies which obligations each tool examines, but two checks can still share a blind spot. A candidate may pass functional simulation, prove a bus-interface assertion, and close timing at a nominal operating point while simultaneous switching causes voltage droop that none of those models includes. An additional check earns its place only by observing a relevant behavior the others leave open.

Different tools do not guarantee independent failure behavior, as multiversion-programming research cautions [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. Language-model evaluators can also favor their own generations [@PanicksseryEtAl2024SelfPreference]. The practical question is which specification assumptions, model simplifications, or learned components the producer and checker share (@fig-independent-checks).

![**A second check adds protection when it can expose a failure the first check could miss.** Sharing a model or specification between producer and critic produces correlated agreement rather than independent validation (left). A claim-specific check using an orthogonal measurement path mounts a bounded challenge, though unexamined shared assumptions must still be recorded (right) [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion; @PanicksseryEtAl2024SelfPreference].](images/fig-independent-checks){#fig-independent-checks width="80%" fig-alt="Two-column flow diagram contrasting correlated agreement from shared assumptions against a bounded challenge from an orthogonal checking path."}

For example, a generated testbench and an assertion suite can agree because both omit backpressure. Their different execution engines do not repair the missing requirement. Applying mutation testing across both checkers can expose a joint escape: a non-equivalent RTL defect survives the assertion suite and the dynamic tests [@DeMilloLiptonSayward1978Hints]. The team then traces the escape through the asserted property, formal assumptions, stimulus, and checked outputs. The two checks may share an omission or miss the fault for different reasons; rerunning the mutant after revision tests whether the specific gap has closed.

Security properties expose a further limit of agreement. Spectre and Meltdown demonstrated leakage through transient execution and microarchitectural side channels that ordinary checks of architectural outputs need not detect [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre; @LippEtAl2018Meltdown]. Two functional suites can therefore agree while leaving information flow unexamined. A relevant challenge might instead use a noninterference proof under declared speculative semantics, cache-timing-channel analysis, or a domain-isolation check matched to the threat model. The choice follows the missing obligation, not the number of tools already reporting a pass. The broader use of such challenges to evaluate and harden the complete design system belongs to @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect; here, their role is to qualify the findings that drive its next action.

## Routing Results to Design Actions {#sec-routing-evidence-layers}

A qualified finding should identify both the affected object and the next action. A formal counterexample may implicate the RTL, the specification, or an abstraction; negative timing slack calls for diagnosis before choosing a repair; an unresolved latency difference may call for more measurement rather than a new cache. Collapsing these returns into one optimizer score discards the information needed to act on them. The routing rule is therefore status first, affected object second, and action third (@tbl-feedback-destinations).

| **Established status** | **Affected object** | **Eligible next action** |
| - | - | - |
| **Execution failure** | Tool setup or runtime environment | Repair the environment and retry; do not label the candidate defective. |
| **Qualified violation** | RTL, physical implementation, or intended contract | Diagnose the cause, repair within the allowed scope, and rerun affected checks. |
| **Proved property** | Scoped verification obligation | Record the discharged obligation with its model and assumptions. |
| **Proxy outside support** | Proxy or its qualification study | Obtain reference measurements, narrow use, replace the proxy, or stop using it. |
| **Missing constraint** | Study formulation or representation | Add and justify the missing constraint; re-evaluate affected candidates. |
| **Resolved outcome, open mechanism** | Proposed explanation | Preserve the outcome and add a distinguishing contrast before attributing its cause. |
| **Unresolved comparison** | Measurement plan | Investigate under the declared plan, or define a new comparison with its own budget and stopping rule. |
| **Difference below decision margin** | Study findings | Retain the result without forcing an architectural change. |
| **Accepted bounded exception** | Requirement and responsible owner | Record waiver scope, rationale, compensating control, and reopening trigger. |
: **The same tool can return findings that require different actions.** Routing preserves the distinction between repairing execution, changing the design, improving a check, and retaining a bounded finding. {#tbl-feedback-destinations tbl-colwidths="[25,30,45]"}

The first two rows illustrate the cost of confusing status with cause. Retrying after a license failure may recover a missing result; retrying an unchanged design under the same valid timing conditions does not repair a setup violation. Likewise, a counterexample becomes a qualified violation only after the reachability and realizability checks in @tbl-formal-result-status establish what failed.

Conflicting checks require diagnosis before they justify a design change. If a formal run reports Proved while simulation shows a miscompare, the team must determine whether the proof covers the failing behavior under the simulation's inputs and assumptions. If two proxies reverse the ranking of a candidate pair, their reference agreement, scope, and uncertainty need examination. Both returns remain in the record with their limits, while the disputed behavior or ranking is withheld from training labels. Independently qualified measurements remain usable within their own scope.

For a confirmed physical violation, diagnosis determines how much of the design needs to change. A *causal repair hierarchy* orders possible repairs by their disruption:

1. **Localized physical repairs.** Gate sizing, threshold-voltage ($V_t$) swaps, buffer insertion, and pin swaps can address timing near-misses without changing the RTL or intended sequential behavior. These ECOs still need checks for timing, power, and other affected requirements.
2. **Retiming and pipelining.** Moving registers or adding stages changes the sequential implementation. SEC must check the intended cycle correspondence; added latency is permissible only where the interface contract allows it.
3. **Structural redesign.** Decomposing a wide arbiter or replacing a monolithic crossbar with a distributed NoC can address a bottleneck that local repair cannot remove. Such changes can invalidate floorplans, interface assumptions, and earlier proofs.

This ordering does not require trying every local repair before redesign. An interface bandwidth limit may rule out a local fix, while the power cost of an ECO may make stopping the better choice. The allowed actions also matter: a Layer 2 search inside a fixed parameter template cannot invent a microarchitecture outside that template. A prospective Layer 3 system would need representations and checks that permit structural changes. Both can read detailed signoff reports; broader action scope does not make those reports stronger evidence (@sec-three-operational-layers). Whether automated repair improves on conventional engineering remains a separate matched comparison.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Drive actions only from qualified results"}
**The principle:** A returned result should change only the design, check, or search state that its qualified meaning supports.

**The application:** A confirmed violation can justify repair, an unresolved comparison can justify further measurement, and an admitted observation can update a search model under its declared rule. An infrastructure failure or unsupported proxy score must not become a verified hardware label.
:::

A confirmed violation may receive a bounded waiver as an alternative to repair. Siemens Calibre Auto-Waivers provides an example of retaining geometric design-rule waivers across layout iterations [@SiemensCalibreAutoWaivers]. Each accepted exception still needs its technical rationale, affected rule and design scope, compensating controls, responsible owner, and reopening trigger. The waiver records an accepted exception rather than an unconditional pass. Repair, waiver, or no change then becomes part of what the project retains, alongside the evidence that justified it.

## Learning Within and Across Design Runs {#sec-propagating-feedback-optimizer}

A useful result can improve work at three horizons. For the next run, a verified timing failure may steer the search away from an infeasible region or motivate a diagnostic check. Within the current project, the same result records a physical limit, the attempted repair, and the obligations still open. For future work, the valuable asset may be the test that caught the defect or the conditions under which a proxy failed, rather than a winning configuration. Learning therefore includes better checks and retained engineering knowledge as well as updated model weights.

These uses require different records. The design findings preserve what was checked, including failed and inconclusive outcomes with their scope and assumptions. The search state records which qualified observations influenced later proposals. A transient tool failure can inform runtime recovery without becoming a negative hardware example, and an unsupported surrogate score cannot become a reference label merely because it was saved [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden; @Settles2009ActiveLearning].

Within the active search, routine adaptation differs from replacing the method. A Bayesian optimizer that updates its posterior after an admitted measurement follows its declared update rule; it does not need a separate promotion study after every observation. Changing the surrogate family, generator prompt, or search policy instead changes the method being evaluated. The proposed replacement needs a comparison suited to its job before adoption: prediction and screening quality for a surrogate, or candidate quality and total evaluation cost for a generator or policy. Retaining the current version remains a valid outcome.

The cases used for that comparison also need protection. Repeatedly choosing model versions against the same holdout leaks information through the choices even if its examples never enter training. Fresh confirmation cases, limits on adaptive reuse, or an inference procedure designed for reuse are needed to preserve the intended comparison [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout]. Version identities make these changes traceable; they do not establish technical validity.

Qualification can also expire while the method remains unchanged. A *distribution shift* changes the distribution of workloads or candidate designs relative to the data used to qualify a model [@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift]. Tool revisions and new PVT conditions can likewise change the relationship between a candidate and its measured behavior. A known change is reason to revisit the affected check immediately rather than wait for an error monitor to alarm. New reference measurements must test whether the proxy still supports its intended use.

The calibration limits from @sec-support-limits apply here. Standard conformal guarantees do not automatically extend to shifted inputs or adaptively selected finalists, and widening an interval by hand does not restore a lost guarantee. Empirical error and coverage checks can reveal deterioration, but they observe only candidates sent to reference tools. Requalification must therefore consider the changed conditions and unsampled regions as well as the monitored returns (@tbl-proxy-diagnostics).

The resulting evidence can improve the project even when no new design is accepted. A disproved mechanism narrows the next experiment; a surviving mutant identifies a weakness in the tests; a comparison inside the decision margin supports retaining the current architecture. These findings, together with their conditions and reopening triggers, are what later work can examine for reuse. Whether they transfer to a different design problem is the next chapter's question (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack), rather than a consequence of saving them.

## Open Questions {#sec-feedback-open-questions}

The qualification discipline developed in this chapter exposes five open research problems as automated search alters the candidates, interfaces, and failure modes under test:

- **When an optimizer pushes designs right up to the clock-timing limit, how do we keep a fast timing model from letting failing paths slip through?** Standard regression losses and split-conformal intervals treat 50\ ps of optimism and 50\ ps of pessimism as equally bad, yet in hardware screening an optimistic error lets a setup violation pass while a pessimistic error merely rejects a borderline candidate or triggers an extra static-timing run. Because an optimizer actively hunts for candidates pressed against the zero-slack boundary, it systematically picks designs where the predictor was overly optimistic, breaking the exchangeability assumption behind standard coverage guarantees. We still lack practical ways to build one-sided calibration bounds and targeted reference-sampling rules that limit false passes along an active search frontier. Such methods would keep pre-signoff screening reliable without mistaking a calibrated surrogate for a signoff static timing analyzer.

- **When a model helps write both the hardware and the testbench, how do we catch the blind spots they share?** Joint mutation testing can expose bugs that slip past both a dynamic simulation testbench and a formal assertion suite, but small syntax mutants injected into an existing AST still share any specification omission inherited by both the RTL and its checkers. Independent development alone does not ensure independent failures. The launch-interceptor experiment found dependent failures among separately developed programs even after the researchers had revised the shared requirements to address ambiguities found in an earlier experiment [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. That correlated failure risk sharpens when a language model drafts an RTL module alongside its testbench or SVA properties, or when a structural search introduces an interface protocol that the original verification plan never anticipated. We still need specification-level fault models and independent contract-synthesis methods that test shared assumptions directly and place statistical bounds on the bugs that remain beyond a finite set of injected mutants.

- **How can we catch dangerous power-up current spikes at the RTL or floorplan stage, before a full physical layout exists?** Static UPF checks and low-power RTL simulations quickly verify isolation clamping and power-state tables, but they cannot see the inrush currents, ground bounce, and dynamic voltage droop that occur when multiple power domains wake up simultaneously. Because a structural search cannot afford full-chip place-and-route and dynamic IR-drop simulation on every proposed power-domain partition, it needs a fast way to rule out electrically unsafe wakeup schedules early. We do not yet have conservative pre-layout current-envelope models that can flag hazardous domain-transition sequences at RTL or floorplan time while clearly marking the switching regimes where the early bound is inconclusive and full physical signoff must run.

- **When a check fails at the boundary between two hardware blocks, how can an automated repair loop tell whether the bug lies inside one block or in the interface contract between them?** In compositional assume-guarantee verification, a counterexample trace at a module boundary can stem from an internal state-machine bug, an upstream driver violating its assumed traffic envelope, or an interface contract that is too weak to prevent deadlock under realistic backpressure. Patching a block's local RTL when the contract itself is flawed wastes synthesis cycles and risks breaking neighboring blocks, whereas escalating every assertion failure to a full interface redesign destroys modularity. We still lack diagnostic synthesis and counterfactual trace-slicing methods that can tell when a violation can be fixed strictly inside a block's existing contract and when the system must instead renegotiate the assume-guarantee boundary across adjacent subsystems.

- **When several verification tools overlap in what they test, how do we decide whether running one more checker is worth the compute and license cost?** Adding a formal property engine, a mutation-testing pass, or an extra timing corner can catch defects that earlier stages missed. Each added check, however, consumes compute servers and commercial license seats, partially duplicates existing coverage, and introduces its own false rejections. Because checkers often share specification assumptions, simple majority voting among evaluators can reinforce a shared blind spot rather than reduce risk, and historical fault-kill ratios measured on baseline designs often break down once a generator shifts the candidate distribution. We still lack practical verification scheduling rules that estimate how much new evidence an extra check will provide on the current candidate, allocating tool budgets to balance missed-defect risk against false-rejection cost.

## Summary {#sec-trust-boundary-conclusion}

A tool return becomes usable architectural evidence when its candidate identity, operating conditions, execution status, and observational scope support the claim being made. For a formal result, qualification binds the property to its model, assumptions, and proof status; for a comparative measurement, it also requires a matched comparator, any relevant uncertainty, and a declared decision margin. That separation lets an architect preserve a valid proof even when a performance comparison remains unresolved, or retain a measured latency gain without claiming unbounded correctness.

Once a return is qualified, its status determines the eligible next action. A formal counterexample can justify an RTL repair or a revised architectural proposal, an unresolved comparison can justify collecting more measurements under the declared plan, and a discrepancy between checkers calls for diagnosis before either result changes the design. Learning then operates across three horizons: guiding the next proposal or check within the active run, updating the findings retained across the project, and carrying proven checks or calibration limits forward to later studies. Within a run, routine updates follow the declared method, whereas proposed replacement models or policies require evaluation before adoption. Unsupported surrogate scores are never treated as verified training labels. Each retained finding carries the conditions under which it can be examined for reuse.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Repair needs both an available action and evidence to assess it.** The represented search space determines which changes a loop can propose. Scalar scores can rank those proposals, while structured diagnostics add context for diagnosis. A proposed structural repair still needs checks of its intended effect and the requirements it may invalidate.
- **A suite's fault sensitivity must be tested.** Use claim-specific verification paths and seeded faults to test whether agreement reflects genuine fault detection. Detecting the tested mutants leaves shared omissions and untested faults open.
- **Only qualified returns should drive the next action.** Admit measurements under the criteria of @tbl-measurement-record and formal returns under their property, model, assumptions, and status, and route each according to the scoped claim it supports. License preemption, cluster timeouts, and environment crashes route to environment repair rather than becoming false design failures.
- **Proof and measurement answer different questions.** A completed unbounded proof establishes that an invariant holds across all reachable states within its declared assumptions. A comparative trade-off needs matched conditions, qualified workload and model scope, and a decision margin declared before measurement. Sampling or run variation also requires appropriate uncertainty characterization, such as a confidence interval; an exact deterministic score does not require a sampling interval.
- **Updating the search is a different job from retaining evidence.** Preserve checked findings with their conditions, and record how they update the search. Separate ordinary adaptation under the declared method from proposed model or policy replacements, whose benefit still needs evaluation.
:::

Qualifying tool returns and updating search state keeps a design loop honest within a project. When a new project changes the workload, compiler toolchain, or process node, the architect faces a question of transfer across design problems: which prior models, checks, and conclusions remain valid, and where do changed conditions require fresh evidence (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack)?
